newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Kabila blocks U.N. path to alleged massacre sites.
newsitem.headline: Kabila blocks U.N. path to alleged massacre sites.

text.p: President Laurent Kabila has blocked the U.N.'s path to alleged massacre sites in the jungles of former Zaire, but investigators said on Monday they would not pull out of the country immediately.

An advance U.N. team in the capital Kinshasa said on Sunday that the government had rejected two non-negotiable terms for the investigation, set down in April in a resolution of the U.N. Commission on Human Rights.
"We need the full cooperation of the authorities. At present the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo is not prepared to accept the investigation," spokesman John Mills told Reuters.

The mission follows allegations that Kabila's Tutsi-backed rebels or their Rwandan or Ugandan allies killed an unknown number of Rwandan Hutu refugees as they marched across Zaire before toppling president Mobutu Sese Seko in May.
Some reports say the killings have continued as the last bands of refugees -- some of them armed Hutus responsible for the 1994 genocide of Tutsis back home -- are tracked down.
The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees says 250,000 Hutus who had lived in camps in Zaire since 1994 are unaccounted for. Another 800,000 went home after their camps were overrun.
Mills said on Monday the advance team would press on with a meeting with officials on Tuesday to discuss the security and free movement investigators will need, if they ever start work.
The main body of researchers was due to arrive on July 7 but is unlikely to make it, he said. A previous attempt to visit the country in May was also blocked.
The Washington Post said this month Kabila had told local officials not to help the U.N. investigation.
Kabila denies this, and says there were no massacres and that there are no more refugees. Aid workers say there are.
Officials of the renamed Congo rejected any investigation led by Roberto Garreton, the U.N. Special Rapporteur for human rights in ex-Zaire who was also a persona non grata for Mobutu.
"They do not believe Garreton is objective. We do not agree of course," Mills said.
Kinshasa also wants the investigation to look only at what happened up to May 17 -- the day Kabila took power -- and to include alleged ethnic killings carried out since 1993 under Mobutu.
But the U.N. resolution covers alleged massacres since last September, when Kabila's uprising was beginning, to now.
Only the U.N. Commission on Human Rights, which meets each year in March and April, can amend the resolution its 53 member states passed unanimously in April.
"Special sessions can be called but there has to be an interest in doing so first," Mills said.
Congo officials were not immediately available for comment.
Kabila's soldiers include many Tutsis, the rivals of the Hutus.
The minority Tutsis took control of Rwanda in a 1994 war during which Hutus systematically killed up to one million Tutsis and moderate Hutu opponents, before fleeing into neighbouring countries.
